summary: Describes a general mechanism that lets other protocols derive their own keying material from a TLS session, after TLS has done the key establishment. This avoids reinventing key exchange. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A TLS exporter lets an application derive keying material from a TLS session instead of establishing a separate key exchange. A label and optional context distinguish the material used for different purposes.

questions: what are tls keying material exporters
how to derive keys from a tls session
what is a tls keying material exporter
subtitle: How an application derives its own keying material from an established TLS session.

tldr.problem: Some protocols use TLS or DTLS to establish keys, then need separate keying material for their own purposes.
tldr.mechanism: An exporter takes a label, an optional application context value, and an output length. It uses the TLS pseudorandom function with the session master secret and random values to produce keying material.
tldr.outcome: Different labels separate different uses of the output. RFC 5705 is updated by RFC 8446, RFC 8447, and RFC 9846.

today: RFC 5705 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2010. It has been updated by RFC 8446, RFC 8447, and RFC 9846.

sections.title: Why Export Keying Material
sections.content:
Some protocols use Transport Layer Security (TLS) or Datagram TLS (DTLS) to establish keys, then use some of that keying material for another purpose. The RFC gives DTLS-SRTP as an example: DTLS establishes keys and negotiates the SRTP protection suite, then the protocol uses the DTLS master secret to generate SRTP keys.

The RFC calls the exported output Exported Keying Material (EKM). The exporter mechanism is compatible with all TLS versions described by the document.
sections.plainLanguage: An application can use TLS to establish shared secrets, then derive additional keying material from that session. The exporter gives applications a common method for doing this.

sections.title: Requirements for Exported Values
sections.content:
The exporter must let both the client and server obtain the same EKM value. To an attacker who does not know the master secret, that value should be indistinguishable from random data.

A single TLS or DTLS association should support multiple exported values. Knowing one EKM value should not reveal useful information about the master secret or other EKM values.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides need to derive the same value, while an outsider should not be able to predict it. Learning one exported value should not reveal the session secret or other exported values.

sections.title: Agreeing on the Application Context
sections.content:
Applications must securely establish the context where exported keys will be used. Context can include the algorithms, parameters, endpoint identifiers, session identifiers, and key lifetimes. The RFC does not prescribe one way to agree on this information.

Possible methods include putting context in the exporter's optional data, exchanging it in TLS extensions, or using a separate upper-layer handshake protected by the exported keys. The context must identify the application through a disambiguating label. Embedding TLS messages in another protocol does not automatically secure all context information, because those upper-layer messages are not covered by the TLS Finished messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Both applications must agree what the exported key is for and which settings go with it. The label identifies the application, while other context details need their own secure agreement.

sections.title: Inputs to the Exporter
sections.content:
An exporter takes a label string, a per-association context value, and a length. It produces a pseudorandom bit string of the requested length from the TLS master secret. The output is scoped to the TLS session, label, and context value.

Without a context value, the TLS pseudorandom function uses the label and the client and server random values. With a context, the construction also includes the context value's length and its contents. The context length is an unsigned 16-bit quantity, and the context may be zero length.

Labels beginning with EXPERIMENTAL may be used privately without registration. Other labels MUST be registered through Specification Required. Labels SHOULD begin with EXPORTER to reduce collisions with other pseudorandom-function labels.
sections.plainLanguage: The exporter combines the session secret with a label, optional context, and requested length. Changing the label or context changes which application-specific value the peers derive.

sections.title: Keeping Exported Values Independent
sections.content:
Exporter outputs need to remain independent. Even if an attacker chooses several label and context pairs and sees their outputs, the output for a different pair should look random. The RFC says the current TLS pseudorandom functions are believed to meet this goal if the master secret is randomly generated.

The same label applied to the same master secret produces the same value, so values with one label must not be reused for different purposes. The RFC also warns that some cipher suites can allow two sessions to share a master secret under particular conditions. Applications need to consider this when using EKM, and new exporter uses should receive careful review.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications should use distinct labels for distinct purposes and should not assume every TLS session has a unique master secret. A secure protocol using exported values still needs careful design.

sections.title: The Exporter Label Registry
sections.content:
The RFC establishes a TLS Exporter Label registry. Several initial labels are reserved because they already serve a similar but distinct purpose in TLS and MUST NOT be used for this exporter mechanism. Other initial entries are associated with EAP-TLS and EAP-TTLS.

New labels are allocated under the Specification Required policy. Labels use printable ASCII characters, and IANA must check that one label is not a prefix of another.
sections.plainLanguage: A registry helps applications choose labels without collisions. Some labels are reserved for other TLS functions, and future labels need a specification.

viz.caption: EXPORTER COMPUTATION WITH CONTEXT FROM SECTION 4

data.title: Exporter inputs
data.code:
PRF(master_secret, label,
    client_random + server_random +
    context_value_length + context_value)[length]
